prompt: We're planning next year's roadmap for Nordic Freight and the whole argument is about where to invest. Repo at <fixtures>/nordic-freight — docs/domain has the model and the business model. Give me the strategic read on which parts of the domain deserve the effort.
trap: Four of the seven contexts are already labelled core, Invoicing among them, and Invoicing carries by far the largest model (5 aggregates, 34 tables). Two tempting failures: accepting the existing labels as the classification, and reading Invoicing's mass as evidence that it is both complex and important — inferring differentiation from code size, which is exactly backwards.
expected_output: A Core Domain Chart placing all seven contexts on complexity × differentiation, with Consolidation identified as the real core and Invoicing as a low-differentiation cost sink, plus an explicit investment-mismatch report using the mass figures and a proposed delta for the contexts whose subdomain_type disagrees with the chart.

assertions.text: A two-axis Core Domain Chart (model complexity × business differentiation) is produced with every context placed
Invoicing is placed at low differentiation on business evidence (the business model states nobody chose Nordic for its invoices), not on its table count
Consolidation is identified as the highest-differentiation context, citing the Guaranteed Consolidation premium as evidence
The investment mismatch is stated explicitly with the mass numbers on both sides (Invoicing 34 tables / 5 aggregates vs Consolidation 5 tables / 1 aggregate)
Invoicing's complexity is questioned as potentially accidental (eleven years of growth, three aggregates modelling VAT variation) rather than accepted as essential domain complexity
Disagreements with the existing subdomain_type labels are surfaced as proposed deltas; the fixture's model.yaml files are not edited
The result does not leave four contexts classified as core
